items.prompt: What is the main reason a species is officially declared extinct?

options.label: When its population becomes very small
options.feedback: A small population is alarming, but extinction means there are no living individuals left anywhere, not just a few.

options.label: When no living individuals of that species remain anywhere
options.feedback: That is the definition: a species is extinct when the last member has died and none are left in the wild or in captivity.

options.label: When it cannot be found in one particular region
options.feedback: Being absent from a region is called local extinction or extirpation; the species may still live elsewhere.

options.label: When its habitat is destroyed
options.feedback: Habitat destruction threatens a species and can lead to extinction, but it is a cause, not the definition of extinction itself.

items.ko_line: Extinction is about having zero individuals.
items.exp_text: A species is extinct when every single individual has died and none survive anywhere on Earth. It is not about being rare, being missing from one area, or having a damaged habitat—those are serious problems that can lead to extinction, but extinction itself is the complete and permanent end of that kind of animal.

items.prompt: Where did the dodo live before it disappeared?

options.label: On the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean
options.feedback: That is correct—the dodo was found only on Mauritius, a remote island, and nowhere else.

options.label: On the islands of the Caribbean Sea
options.feedback: The Caribbean had its own extinct birds, but the dodo was not one of them; it belonged to Mauritius.

options.label: On the island of Madagascar off Africa
options.feedback: Madagascar had giant extinct birds like the elephant bird, but the dodo lived on Mauritius, not Madagascar.

options.label: On the islands of the Pacific Ocean
options.feedback: Pacific islands had their own unique birds, but the dodo's home was in the Indian Ocean, on Mauritius.

items.ko_line: The dodo was not from those islands.
items.exp_text: The dodo lived only on the island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean. Because it had no natural predators there, it lost the ability to fly and nested on the ground, which made it easy prey for sailors and the animals they brought, and it disappeared within a century of their arrival.

items.prompt: What was the passenger pigeon's main food source that helped it gather in such enormous flocks?

options.label: Fish from rivers and lakes
options.feedback: Passenger pigeons were land birds and ate plant food, not fish; fish-eating birds have different beaks and habits.

options.label: Small insects caught in mid-air
options.feedback: Insects were not their staple; they were seed-eaters, and their beaks were built for cracking nuts and grains.

options.label: Acorns, beechnuts, and other forest seeds
options.feedback: That is right—they followed the seasonal bursts of acorns and beechnuts in eastern North American forests, which allowed millions to gather where food was dense.

options.label: Leaves and tender shoots from bushes
options.feedback: Leaves are not their main diet; they preferred the energy-rich seeds of forest trees, which let huge flocks stay together.

items.ok_line: Forest seeds drew the huge flocks.
items.ko_line: They ate seeds, not fish or leaves.
items.exp_text: Passenger pigeons fed mainly on the seeds of forest trees, especially acorns and beechnuts. These seeds ripened in massive quantities in the same woods, so the birds could gather by the millions to feast; this dependence on a few nut crops is also why they moved constantly and nested in dense colonies.

items.prompt: What feature of the great auk's body made it a strong swimmer but unable to fly?

options.label: Its long, pointed tail
options.feedback: A long tail helps steering but does not prevent flight; many flying birds have long tails.

options.label: Its large, webbed feet
options.feedback: Webbed feet aid swimming but are common in flying birds like ducks, so they do not explain flightlessness.

options.label: Its light, hollow bones
options.feedback: Hollow bones are typical of flying birds; the great auk had heavier, solid bones that helped it dive but weighed it down.

options.label: Its short, stubby wings used as flippers
options.feedback: That is the key—its wings were small and stiff, perfect for paddling underwater but far too short and heavy to lift its body into the air.

items.ko_line: It was the wings that stopped flight.
items.exp_title: Why the great auk couldn't fly
items.exp_text: The great auk's wings were short, dense, and used like flippers to propel it through the water after fish. That made it an excellent diver but meant it could not take off, leaving it helpless when hunters came to its nesting beaches—it could only waddle or swim away slowly.

items.prompt: Why did the Steller's sea cow stay so close to the shore where it was easy for hunters to reach?

options.label: It was chasing fish that came near the beach
options.feedback: Steller's sea cows ate plants, not fish, so they had no reason to chase prey; they stayed near shore to feed on seaweed.

options.label: It fed on seaweed growing in the shallow water near the coast
options.feedback: That is correct—it grazed on kelp and other seaweeds in shallow coastal waters, so it rarely went far out to sea.

options.label: It was escaping from sharks in deeper water
options.feedback: There is no evidence it hid from sharks; it simply lived where its food grew, which was in the shallows.

options.label: It came ashore to rest and warm up in the sun
options.feedback: It was a fully aquatic mammal and could not move well on land; it did not come ashore habitually.

items.ko_line: It was feeding, not hiding or resting.
items.exp_text: The Steller's sea cow was a plant-eater that fed on the thick seaweed beds growing in the shallow waters along the coast. That kept it always within easy reach of shore, where hunters in boats could approach and kill it without the animal being able to dive deep or swim away fast.

items.prompt: What made the quagga's stripes different from those of other zebras?

options.label: Its stripes were only on the front half of its body, fading to plain brown at the rear
options.feedback: That is right—the quagga had stripes on its head, neck, and shoulders, but its back half was mostly a plain sandy brown, unlike other zebras.

options.label: Its stripes were vertical instead of horizontal
options.feedback: Zebra stripes are generally vertical on the front and horizontal on the legs; the quagga's oddity was not their direction but where they stopped.

options.label: Its stripes were white on a black background
options.feedback: All zebras, including the quagga, have dark stripes over a lighter base; the quagga's difference was the pattern's coverage, not its colour contrast.

options.label: Its stripes were completely absent
options.feedback: The quagga did have stripes, but only on part of its body; a completely stripe-less zebra would be a different animal.

items.ok_line: Stripes only on the front half.
items.ko_line: It had stripes, just not everywhere.
items.exp_text: The quagga looked like a zebra from the front, with dark stripes on its head and neck, but from the shoulders back it had a plain brown coat like a horse or donkey. This unique pattern made it look like a cross between a zebra and a horse, and it lived on the grasslands of South Africa until it was hunted to extinction in the late 1800s.

items.prompt: Why were Caribbean monk seals so easy for hunters to approach on the beaches where they rested?

options.label: They were blind and could not see people coming
options.feedback: They had normal eyesight; their vulnerability came from their behaviour, not from being unable to see.

options.label: They were too heavy to move at all on land
options.feedback: They could move on land, though clumsily; the problem was that they did not flee when humans approached, not that they were immobile.

options.label: They had no fear of humans and did not flee when approached
options.feedback: That is correct—having evolved on islands without land predators, they showed no fear of people, so hunters could walk right up and club them.

options.label: They slept so deeply that they could not be awakened
options.feedback: They could wake up, but they did not run away; their lack of fear, not deep sleep, made them easy targets.

items.ko_line: It was their tameness, not any disability.
items.exp_title: Why the monk seal was easy prey
items.exp_text: Caribbean monk seals grew up on islands where there were no natural land predators, so they never learned to be afraid of large animals like humans. When sailors arrived, the seals simply lay on the beach and let people walk up to them, making it easy for hunters to kill them for their oil and meat, and they were gone by the 1950s.

items.prompt: Why couldn't the Xerces blue butterfly caterpillars simply move to a different plant when their original food plant disappeared?

options.label: They were too weak to crawl to another plant
options.feedback: Caterpillars can crawl, but the real issue is that they would not eat the wrong plant even if they reached it.

options.label: They only ate one kind of plant and did not recognise others as food
options.feedback: That is essentially correct—their caterpillars were specialists that would only feed on the specific plant they were born on, so when that plant vanished, they starved.

options.label: They were eaten by birds before they could move
options.feedback: Predation was a risk, but the main barrier was dietary: the caterpillars could not switch to other plants at all.

options.label: They could not move because the plant was removed entirely
options.feedback: This is close but not the whole story; even if there were other plants nearby, the caterpillars would not eat them because they were specialised.

items.ok_line: One plant was their only food.
items.ko_line: They would not eat other plants.
items.exp_title: A butterfly tied to one plant
items.exp_text: The Xerces blue butterfly's caterpillars fed only on the lupine plant that grew in the sandy coastal dunes near San Francisco. When urban development destroyed those dunes and the lupines disappeared, the caterpillars had no alternative food source, because their bodies were not built to digest or accept other plants, and the species went extinct in the 1940s.

items.prompt: Why does a Baiji, a river dolphin, rely mainly on sound rather than eyesight to find its way and hunt?

options.label: It is completely blind from birth
options.feedback: It is not blind, but its eyes are small and weak; the real reason is that the river water is too murky to see through.

options.label: The Yangtze River water is too muddy for vision to be useful
options.feedback: That is correct—the river carries so much silt that visibility is almost zero, so the dolphin uses echolocation with sound clicks to sense its surroundings and prey.

options.label: It hunts at night when there is no light
options.feedback: It does hunt in dark conditions, but even in daylight the water is too cloudy; sound works regardless of light.

options.label: It lives in the open ocean where sight is useless
options.feedback: The Baiji lives in the Yangtze River, not the open ocean, and the ocean is clearer; its home water is the muddy river.

items.ko_line: It is the water, not night or blindness.
items.exp_text: The Baiji lives in the Yangtze River, which carries so much mud and silt that a dolphin cannot see more than a short distance ahead. To find fish and avoid obstacles, it sends out high-pitched clicks and listens to the echoes, a method called echolocation that works perfectly even in water too cloudy for eyes.

items.prompt: How did male Pyrenean ibex most likely use their large curved horns during the mating season?

options.label: They fought each other by clashing horns to win the right to mate
options.feedback: That is correct—males would rear up and slam their heavy curved horns against each other in contests, and the winner gained access to females.

options.label: They used them to dig for roots and tubers
options.feedback: Ibex are grazers and browsers that eat plants above ground; their horns are for fighting, not digging.

options.label: They used them to defend against predators like wolves
options.feedback: Horns could be used in defence, but their main and most important use was in male-to-male combat during breeding, not against predators.

options.label: They used them to break ice on frozen water sources
options.feedback: There is no evidence they broke ice with horns; their winter survival relied on finding exposed vegetation, not cracking ice.

items.ko_line: They were for fighting rivals, not chores.
items.exp_text: During the breeding season, male Pyrenean ibex competed for females by standing on their hind legs and crashing their large curved horns together in powerful clashes. The strongest and most skilled fighter usually won the right to mate, which is why these horns were so large and important for the species, even though it is now extinct.
